title: Monetary policy statement and Q&A — Christine Lagarde and Boris Vujčić
summary: A hold can preserve a tightening bias. On 29 October some members of the ECB Governing Council saw a case for an immediate increase, yet the eventual decision to hold was unanimous. Two developments since the September projections pulled in opposite directions. Energy had become sufficiently expensive to raise the risk that inflation would stay above target for longer. At the same time, average ten-year sovereign yields had risen about 35 basis points since the September projection cut-off, tightening financial conditions. Lagarde said the direction of the next policy move was clear if incoming information confirmed the current assessment. She declined to specify the decision in December or commit to moving only at quarterly projection meetings (first two policy exchanges and Q&A on the quarterly pace).

The 35 basis points describe a change in sovereign yields over an inter-meeting interval. They do not measure the surprise in the ECB decision on 29 October. Nor did Lagarde translate that rise into an equivalent change in the policy rate. In response to a question about French bonds, she pointed to a worldwide rise in long rates, citing expected inflation, the anticipated policy path and increased long-maturity debt issuance from large technology businesses. She stopped short of claiming that those issues were already crowding others out. These explanations would imply different exposures for investors. A bond sell-off driven by higher expected overnight rates would price in some future ECB action. A higher return demanded for holding long debt could instead raise the cost of investment without much change in the expected overnight rate (Q&A on French spreads and global yields).

Inflation had accelerated, but different parts of the consumption basket were telling different stories. September headline inflation was 3.8%, up from 3.2% in August. Energy inflation rose from 14.3% to 18.9%, with elevated refining margins helping push diesel and petrol prices to new peaks. Inflation excluding energy rose from 2.1% to 2.3%. That particular measure still includes food. Food inflation increased from 1.1% to 1.3% and services from 3.0% to 3.2%, while goods inflation fell from 1.2% to 1.1%. Measures of underlying inflation in aggregate remained broadly stable despite upward pressure early in the pricing chain. Lagarde already saw more indirect pass-through from energy into other prices. The unresolved question was how much further it would propagate into subsequent price and wage decisions (‘Inflation’ and opening Q&A, including the transcript corrections to the energy comparison).

Labour compensation gave the Council a reason to distinguish that risk from the effects already visible. Compensation per employee grew 3.3% year on year in the second quarter, after 3.6% in the first. Productivity gains restrained unit labour costs. The wage tracker, which measures a different concept, pointed to negotiated pay growth of 2.5% to 2.8% during the remaining months of 2026 and 2.6% on average over the first three quarters of 2027. Short-horizon inflation expectations had risen, but most long-horizon measures stayed near 2%. The September projection already allowed for some second-round effects. Lagarde said the evidence so far gave little indication of an additional material response. Comparing new wage settlements with that baseline, including the opening positions of unions in bargaining, would provide a sharper test than asking whether any salary had risen (‘Inflation’ and first answer on wage evidence).

The importance assigned to underlying inflation was changing with the age of the shock. At its onset the domestic components had little time to react. Several months later, their behaviour could reveal whether an energy-driven price increase was becoming persistent. Before December the Council expected two inflation releases, third-quarter GDP and employment, compensation per employee and negotiated wages, two unemployment readings, two industrial production releases and the November purchasing managers’ surveys. The September and October bank interest-rate statistics would also arrive, alongside new staff projections and likely updated scenarios. Taken together, these releases could separate a change in unit costs from weakened demand or more expensive financing. Lagarde gave underlying inflation particular weight in this next assessment while retaining the inflation outlook and the strength of transmission as joint tests (Q&A on inter-meeting data).

The growth case for waiting did not require the economy already to be contracting. Incoming evidence suggested third-quarter expansion. Services had recovered after the initial shock, AI-related investment was helping parts of manufacturing, digital services and exports, and government infrastructure and defence spending was supporting activity. Unemployment remained 6.4% in August, though growth in both employment and the labour force was subdued. More expensive energy was hurting confidence and real purchasing power. The medium-term recovery in demand rested partly on energy prices gradually easing. Continued supply disruption or an unusually cold winter alongside low gas stocks could undermine that assumption. Global bond-market spillovers and fiscal uncertainty could independently tighten borrowing conditions and cut spending. Those risks reinforced one another for growth while having different implications for inflation (‘Economic activity’ and ‘Risk assessment’).

There was already evidence that higher financing costs reached different borrowers at different speeds. Between meetings interest rates had risen broadly and equities had fallen. The last available corporate loan pricing was for August, when the bank rate remained 3.8% while the cost of market debt rose from 4.0% to 4.1%. Annual bank loan growth slowed from 4.4% in July to 4.2% in both August and September. Corporate bond issuance growth accelerated from 3.5% in July to 3.8% in August and 4.2% in September. Identical September growth rates thus concealed opposite changes in momentum. They were annual rates of change in different instruments, not evidence that one euro of bond issuance replaced one euro of bank lending. Banks tightened corporate standards in the third quarter on concerns about customers’ economic risks. Higher inventory and working-capital needs persisted even as overall loan demand fell, with higher rates a particular reason (‘Financial and monetary conditions’).

Housing supplied a useful contrast. Mortgage rates rose from 3.5% in July to 3.6% in August, mortgage credit growth edged down to 3.0% in September, and surveyed mortgage demand fell substantially. Banks reported unchanged mortgage credit standards. For firms, both lending standards and demand moved against borrowing. For mortgages, the clearest survey change came from borrowers. Tracking only total lending would blur that distinction and obscure how much restraint was coming from prices rather than changes in bank approval standards (‘Financial and monetary conditions’).

The exchange about France also drew a boundary around possible intervention. Lagarde connected higher yields to fiscal choices for heavily indebted governments and retained the ECB’s instruments if disorderly, unwarranted market movements threatened monetary transmission. She offered no spread threshold, announcement of intervention or indication that the French spread alone met the conditions. Asked whether different national declines in sovereign holdings reflected selective support, she described runoff as mechanical and confirmed that maturing bonds were not being replaced. A comparison of holdings across countries therefore needs their actual maturity schedules. Separately, Lagarde announced that she would step down after the February 2027 policy meeting, ahead of her scheduled October term end, and said the succession process had started. She linked the decision to wanting to speak about matters beyond the monetary mandate and anticipated continuity. It was a second piece of conference news, relevant when trying to attribute any intraday asset-price move (Q&A on French bonds, redemptions and succession).

questions.question: Which part of the 35-basis-point rise in long yields restrained demand independently of expected ECB hikes?
questions.detail: Compare maturity-matched sovereign yields, euro overnight-indexed swap forwards, inflation compensation and long issuance across the September cut-off and the conference. Then examine new loan pricing as it became available. A higher term premium or a global supply move could tighten borrowing conditions even if the expected near-term ECB path changed little.

questions.question: Did the wage and price evidence surpass the propagation already in September’s forecast?
questions.detail: Compare third-quarter compensation per employee, productivity and negotiated pay with the contemporaneous wage tracker. Examine services, goods and food separately and keep the energy-excluding index distinct from a measure that also excludes food. Persistent domestic acceleration alongside higher pay would alter the case for tightening more than another increase concentrated in fuel.

questions.question: Was French spread widening a market-wide rate move, national fiscal repricing or impaired transmission?
questions.detail: Compare French debt with comparable German and other sovereign maturities, local bank funding and loan rates. Check actual maturity schedules before interpreting differences in Eurosystem portfolio runoff. This would distinguish refinancing pressure from deterioration in the uniform transmission of the policy stance. The conference supplied neither a quantitative trigger nor a finding of fragmentation.

questions.question: What was already priced before the conditional guidance and succession news?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the order of the decision, the early answers about a possible hike and the later answers about succession. Examine meeting-dated swaps, long yields, sovereign spreads and contemporaneous energy quotes separately. A reporter’s reference to a December hike supplies no probability, and a daily closing price cannot identify which of these news items moved markets.
